blocks.content: This closing topic of the Normalization module works through the kind of questions this material commonly gets tested with, identifying which normal form a table violates, normalizing a table to a target form, and explaining the difference between two specific normal forms.

Rather than introducing new concepts, this topic applies 1NF through BCNF, all covered in the earlier topics of this module, to three concrete worked questions, the exact shape these questions tend to take in a real interview.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438692908-26283776.png
1. The Genuinely Common Interview Question Shape
blocks.text: 1. The Genuinely Common Interview Question Shape

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438692909-851195427.png
blocks.alt: The Genuinely Common Interview Question Shape

blocks.content: Normalization interview questions tend to fall into three shapes, given a table, identify which normal form it violates, given a table, normalize it to a specific target form, or explain conceptually what separates two specific normal forms from each other.
2. Worked Question One, Identify the Violation
blocks.text: 2. Worked Question One, Identify the Violation

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438692909-844232920.png
blocks.alt: Worked Question One, Identify the Violation

blocks.content: Question, a table stores order_id alongside product1, product2, and product3 columns to record up to three items per order, which normal form does this violate, and why.

-- Given table
order_id | product1 | product2  | product3
1        | Laptop   | Mouse     | Keyboard
blocks.code:
-- Given table
order_id | product1 | product2  | product3
1        | Laptop   | Mouse     | Keyboard

codes.text:
-- Given table
order_id | product1 | product2  | product3
1        | Laptop   | Mouse     | Keyboard

blocks.content: Answer, this violates 1NF, covered in the earlier First Normal Form topic, the repeating product1, product2, product3 columns are really a hidden list of products forced into a fixed table shape, the fix is a separate order_items table with one row per product.
3. Worked Question Two, Normalize to a Target Form
blocks.text: 3. Worked Question Two, Normalize to a Target Form

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438692910-325497308.png
blocks.alt: Worked Question Two, Normalize to a Target Form

blocks.content: Question, an order_items table has a composite primary key of order_id and product_id, and also includes a customer_name column, which depends only on order_id, normalize this table to 2NF.

Answer, this is a partial dependency, covered in the earlier Second Normal Form topic, customer_name only depends on part of the composite key, the fix moves customer_name into a separate orders table keyed by order_id alone, leaving order_items with only columns that depend on the full composite key.
4. Worked Question Three, Explain the Difference
blocks.text: 4. Worked Question Three, Explain the Difference

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438692910-248801912.png
blocks.alt: Worked Question Three, Explain the Difference

blocks.content: Question, explain the difference between a partial dependency and a transitive dependency, using an example.

{"headers":["Dependency Type","What It Means","Which Normal Form Addresses It"],"rows":[["Partial dependency","A column depends on only part of a composite key","Second Normal Form (2NF)"],["Transitive dependency","A column depends on another non key column, not the key directly","Third Normal Form (3NF)"]]}

Answer, a partial dependency, covered in 2NF, only applies to composite keys, a column depends on part of the key instead of the whole thing, a transitive dependency, covered in 3NF, can happen with any key, a column depends indirectly on the key through some other non key column, department_name depending on department_id which depends on employee_id is the classic transitive example.
5. The Most Common Trap in These Questions
blocks.text: 5. The Most Common Trap in These Questions

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438692910-562485443.png
blocks.alt: The Most Common Trap in These Questions

blocks.content: The single most common mistake in these questions is confusing partial and transitive dependencies, a quick way to tell them apart under pressure, partial dependency questions almost always involve a composite key, transitive dependency questions can involve any key, including a plain single column one.
6. How to Actually Approach These Questions
blocks.text: 6. How to Actually Approach These Questions

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438692911-244464702.png
blocks.alt: How to Actually Approach These Questions

blocks.content: Rather than reciting a memorized definition, working through the actual columns in the given table and asking what each one depends on tends to produce a clearer, more convincing answer, and naturally surfaces the right normal form without needing to guess.

blocks.title: Interviewers usually care more about the reasoning than the label
blocks.content: Correctly identifying the specific dependency, and explaining why it causes a real redundancy problem, generally matters more to an interviewer than simply naming the right normal form.
7. Three Worked Questions, at a Glance

blocks.content: Every one of these worked questions draws directly on the specific topics earlier in this module, Why Normalization, 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF, reviewing those in order is the most direct preparation for this style of question.
8. Common Mistakes
